newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian non-ferrous metals trade seeks duty changes.
newsitem.headline: Indian non-ferrous metals trade seeks duty changes.

text.p: India's non-ferrous metals industry, faced with sluggish demand, has sought protection through higher import duty on semi-finished products in the federal budget, industry officials said on Thursday.
"We have told the Finance Ministry that the difference in import duty between raw materials and semis should be 15 percentage points," Bombay Metal Exchange president Sharad Parikh told Reuters.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to present the 13-party United Front government's second budget to parliament on February 28.
Parikh said duty on semis like pipes, strips, coils and tubes should be 15 percentage points higher than raw material. Currently both carry a uniform duty of 30 percent.
Dealers said industrial users of non-ferrous metals were either importing or buying semi-finished products instead of raw materials which in turn affect the local producers.
As part of economic reforms initiated in 1991, India in March 1992 deregulated metal imports, abolished price controls and cut the import duty on most metals.
The import duty has been brought down to 30 percent from a high of 140 percent during the controlled regime.
Parikh said semi-finished goods manufacturers were cutting down production because they could not compete with imports which turn out to be cheaper due to lower power tariffs and overheads.
"They can keep the semis at the same levels and reduce the duty on raw materials," he said.
Parikh agreed this would badly hit state-run Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL), the country's primary copper producer.
"It is for the government to see how to save HCL," said Parikh.

A senior HCL official said the company had urged the government to raise import duties on copper products to offset losses due to high production costs and a steep fall in London Metal Exchange (LME) prices.
The official said HCL has asked the Mines Ministry to raise the import duty to 60 percent for copper cathodes and wire bars and 65 percent for wire rods from the current 30 percent.
"We are not afraid of competition. But prices have to be competitive," the official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.
"The government can give use relief by way of duty increase," he said. "The government is protecting the other industries, why not copper."
"I think there is a case for increase in duties on copper with a clear message that it is a short-term measure," said A. C. Wadhwan, former chairman of state-run Hindustan Zinc Ltd (HZL).
Wadhwan said the copper industry was in trouble because of a slump in international copper prices to about $2,000 per tonne from $3,000 a year ago. India's metal prices are linked to LME prices.
In 1994/95 India increased duties on copper, lead and zinc by 10 percent but brought it down drastically in 1995/96.
India annually consumes about 200,000 tonnes of copper. HCL produces about 65,000 tonnes annually and the balance is imported.
But Wadhwan said there was no case for changing import duties on zinc and aluminium.
"There is no need to increase duties on zinc because price fluctuation has not been very high. It has ruled between $1,000-1,200 per tonne in the last two years."
Wadhwan said the offtake in the aluminium industry would be low so long as there was an industrial recession. "There is nothing one can do about it."
India's aluminium sector is saddled with inventories after a dip in domestic demand and fall in world aluminium prices.
The demand growth for aluminium in the country in 1996/97 had dropped to about two percent compared to an average eight percent, analysts said.
"The customs duty should be kept at the same level of 30 percent for aluminium and zinc for at least one more year and then reduce it if necessary," he said.

"We presume the government may not reduce any duty on non-ferrous metals but might think of differential duty between semi-finished and raw materials," said Surendra Parikh, a leading Bombay metals trader.
